strengths: Broad empirical validation across five genuinely diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, calcium imaging, TMS-induced E-fields, facial expressions, and monkey motor cortex spiking), which is unusual breadth for a single paper and lends some credibility to the claim of generality.

Reasonably thorough set of ablations: solver-agnosticism (DDIM vs. Rex-RK4, cLDM vs. IsoDiff), kNN vs. MLP lifting decoder, embedding dimensionality sweep (Fig. 10), and comparison against PCA/beta-VAE baselines.

The conceptual separation of 'editing' (in a compact contrastive space) from 'rendering' (in the original diffusion latent space) is a clean and intuitively appealing design, and the algorithmic pipeline (Algorithms 1-2) is spelled out in enough detail to aid reproducibility.

Appendices provide substantial detail on dataset acquisition/simulation (FEM fluid sim, SimNIBS E-field pipeline, DISFA, calcium imaging, MC_Maze), which supports reproducibility for domain-specific parts of the work.
Applications to biomedical/scientific domains (TMS responder/non-responder class transfer, monkey reach kinematics) suggest plausible downstream utility beyond generic image editing.
weaknesses: The PDF itself contains a visibly broken/leftover section (page 8, 'D REVISED RESULTS' with orphaned LaTeX line numbers 1415-1457 and a truncated table) that appears to be an artifact of careless merging/editing. This is a serious presentation defect that raises doubts about how carefully the rest of the submission (and its reported numbers) were checked.

The core technical contribution largely amounts to applying an existing off-the-shelf contrastive method (CEBRA, Schneider et al. 2023) on top of pretrained diffusion latents, combined with standard interpolation/extrapolation tools (cubic splines, finite-difference Taylor expansion, LSTM) and a kNN decoder. Little of this is newly proposed; the novelty is primarily in the systems-level combination and application to diffusion latents rather than in new modeling or theoretical contributions.

Near-zero RMSE values reported for Spline/TEX-2 in C-space (e.g., 0.00 in several rows of Table 1) are suspicious and under-explained: if the spline is fit directly to the full observed embedding sequence and then evaluated at the same points used for fitting (as the interpolation task description suggests: 'we regenerate intermediate frames under observed conditions'), this risks a circular/self-fulfilling comparison rather than a genuine held-out interpolation test. The paper does not clearly clarify whether fitted points are excluded from evaluation.

Despite extensive framing in the introduction and related work around ControlNet, InstructPix2Pix, and NoiseCLR as inadequate baselines, no quantitative head-to-head comparison against these conditioning-based methods is actually presented in the experiments; comparisons are limited to Lerp/Slerp/LSTM/PCA/beta-VAE, which are comparatively weak baselines and may overstate the method's advantage.

Central claims about improved 'interpretability' rest mostly on qualitative visualizations (Fig. 3, Fig. 5) and a single cosine-similarity orthogonality metric (Table 12) rather than systematic quantitative or human-subject evaluation of interpretability, making this core claim less rigorously supported than the fidelity/PSNR claims.

CEBRA-based embedding learning requires per-frame auxiliary labels for every dataset, which is a substantive practical limitation not clearly foregrounded as a core requirement/limitation of the framework (rather than a minor implementation detail), potentially restricting applicability to settings lacking dense auxiliary annotations.

The abstract and results section highlight cherry-picked headline numbers (e.g., '35.7 PSNR vs. 28.3 for linear baselines') without similarly foregrounding weaker results (e.g., calcium imaging RMSE that is often higher, not lower, for Lerp/Slerp vs. ConDA C-space per Table 1, e.g., Ca2+ Lerp RMSE 43.87 in C-space vs. 16.60 in Z-space, an apparent regression that is not discussed).

strengths: Broad empirical scope: the paper validates ConDA on five genuinely diverse spatiotemporal domains (fluid dynamics, two-photon calcium imaging, TMS-induced E-fields, facial action units, and monkey motor cortex spiking), which is an ambitious and useful demonstration of generality.

The dual-space design (lossy, compact contrastive embedding C for editing vs. near-lossless diffusion latent Z for rendering) is a clean and sensible architectural idea that cleanly separates concerns of controllability and fidelity.

Reasonably thorough ablations are included: embedding dimensionality sweep (Fig. 13), comparison against PCA and beta-VAE baselines (Table 2), comparison against CcGAN as an alternative generator backbone (Appendix C.2), and an orthogonality/disentanglement probe (Table 6).

Good engineering/reproducibility documentation in the appendix (detailed simulation protocols for fluid and TMS data, training hyperparameters, parameter counts, and runtime tables), and a promise to open-source code and the fluid benchmark dataset.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core pipeline largely stitches together existing components (DDIM inversion, the CEBRA supervised contrastive encoder from prior work, kNN neighborhood lifting, and standard spline/Taylor/LSTM traversal operators). The paper's own related-work section acknowledges contrastive-learning identifiability results exist, but ConDA provides no new theoretical guarantee or analysis of why/when this composition yields identifiable or dynamics-aligned structure beyond empirical demonstration.

Potential evaluation artifact in Table 1: the near-zero RMSE reported for the Spline method (and very low RMSE for TEX-2) in C-space raises concern about whether the spline is fit to the same points at which it is subsequently evaluated (near-interpolation), which would trivially yield near-zero error regardless of the quality of the underlying representation; the paper does not clarify the train/held-out protocol for this specific metric, undermining confidence in the headline quantitative claims.

The comparison in Fig. 5/Table (monkey reach data) between ConDA (a supervised method using velocity/reach labels) and PCA (a fully unsupervised method) is not apples-to-apples; the improvement could stem largely from the use of label supervision rather than from any specific benefit of contrastive structuring. A supervised linear or regression baseline using the same labels would be a fairer comparison.

Some clinical/scientific claims are overreached relative to the evidence: the TMS responder-classification results are modest (e.g., F1=0.63, small and imbalanced sample of 110 patients, 30 responders vs. 80 non-responders) yet are used to motivate strong claims about a 'tangible path to personalized targeting,' which is not well supported by such modest classification performance.

Reproducibility is uneven across domains: code and the fluid dataset are promised to be released, but the calcium imaging data requires author permission and the TMS patient MRI/HAMD data cannot be released at all (HIPAA), meaning full reproduction of 2 of 5 core experiments is not possible for external reviewers/readers.

The paper's disentanglement/orthogonality evidence (Table 6) is reported for only one dataset (fluid, time vs. Reynolds number) despite the broader claim that latent traversal directions reflect underlying dynamical factors across all five domains; this leaves the generality of the disentanglement claim largely unverified.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy in Section 3, with many overloaded symbols (Z, C, T_eta, h_psi, l, f_theta) introduced in quick succession, which reduces accessibility; some figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 2) are visually cluttered and would benefit from clearer captions tied directly to the metrics reported in the tables.
